claim: ROS 2 Jazzy is the tier-1 ROS 2 distro for Ubuntu 24.04 noble, and Gazebo Harmonic (gz-sim 8) is its default paired Gazebo version supported by ros_gz.
correction: The Gazebo half is exactly right; the "the tier-1 distro" half is overstated by one word. Corrected statement: "ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco (May 2024 - May 2029) is the only LTS distro with Ubuntu 24.04 Noble as a Tier 1 platform. It is not the ONLY Tier 1 distro on Noble — Kilted Kaiju (May 2025 - November 2026, non-LTS) is also Tier 1 [d][a][s] on Noble amd64/arm64 per REP-2000 — but Kilted EOLs in November 2026, so Jazzy remains the correct choice. The current LTS, Lyrical Luth (May 2026), is Tier 1 on Ubuntu 26.04 Resolute and only Tier 3 (source-only) on Noble, so it is not an option on 24.04 without an OS upgrade. Gazebo Harmonic (gz-sim 8, apt metapackage gz-harmonic) is confirmed as Jazzy's officially paired Gazebo: REP-2000's Jazzy dependency table lists Gazebo Harmonic, and ros_gz ships Jazzy+Harmonic on the `jazzy` branch with binaries from packages.ros.org (ros-jazzy-ros-gz). Harmonic is LTS with EOL May 2029 (not Sep 2028 as sometimes quoted).

claim: Gazebo Classic 11 has no official Ubuntu 24.04 (noble) binary packages and reached end-of-life in January 2025.
correction: Both halves hold up under direct inspection of the primary package repositories. Two precision notes, neither of which changes the verdict: (1) The EOL date is officially listed as 2025-01-29 on classic.gazebosim.org's release table; Open Robotics' public messaging said "as of Friday, January 31st, 2025", and the formal Discourse announcement post ("Gazebo Classic 11 has reached end-of-life", by azeey) was published 2025-02-03, the same day the gazebosim/gazebo-classic GitHub repo was archived. So "January 2025" is correct, but pick 2025-01-29 if you need a single canonical date. (2) "No official noble binaries" should not be read as "binaries vanished" — OSRF explicitly stated Gazebo Classic binaries "will not suddenly disappear", and gazebo11/libgazebo11/libgazebo11-dev are still served today for focal (20.04) from packages.osrfoundation.org. The last-ever official Gazebo Classic 11 packaging is: OSRF repo -> bionic/focal only; Ubuntu archive -> jammy universe (gazebo 11.10.2+dfsg-1). Nothing for noble from either source. Practical consequence for this project: on Ubuntu 24.04 there is no apt path to Gazebo Classic at all, so the simulator choice is effectively Gazebo Sim (Harmonic, gz-harmonic, which IS in the OSRF noble repo and is the ROS 2 Jazzy pairing) or a source build / container.
evidence:
DIRECT REPOSITORY INSPECTION (run 2026-07-24, from the target machine):

1. OSRF apt repo, ubuntu-stable, noble — dists/noble/main/binary-amd64/Packages.gz contains 540 packages; grep for '^Package: gazebo11|gazebo9|gazebo$|libgazebo' returns ZERO Gazebo Classic packages. The only simulator metapackage present is gz-harmonic (plus gz-jetty-*, libsdformat14/15/16, dart, etc.).
2. Same check on the non-stable OSRF 'ubuntu' repo for noble: also zero Gazebo Classic packages.
3. Control/sanity check — OSRF ubuntu-stable focal DOES still carry: gazebo11, gazebo11-common, gazebo11-dbg, gazebo11-doc, gazebo11-plugin-base, libgazebo11, libgazebo11-dev (and gazebo9-*). So the absence in noble is real, not a fetch artifact.
4. OSRF ubuntu-stable jammy also has NO gazebo11 (only gz-fortress/garden/harmonic/ionic + sdformat). Confirms OSRF stopped shipping Classic binaries after focal.
5. Ubuntu primary archive, noble: packages.ubuntu.com search for names containing "gazebo" in suite noble -> "Sorry, your search gave no results". Launchpad API getPublishedSources?source_name=gazebo&exact_match=true&distro_series=.../noble -> {"total_size": 0, "entries": []}. So Ubuntu 24.04 universe has no gazebo source or binary package at all.
6. Control check — Ubuntu jammy archive DOES have gazebo 11.10.2+dfsg-1 (universe): gazebo, gazebo-common, gazebo-doc, gazebo-plugin-base, libgazebo-dev, libgazebo11.

7. classic.gazebosim.org (official Gazebo Classic site) states verbatim: "This version of Gazebo, now called Gazebo classic, reaches end-of-life in January 2025." Its release table row reads: "Gazebo 11.0  2020-01-30  EOL 2025-01-29", and lists supported platforms for Gazebo 11 as "Ubuntu B,F" (Bionic, Focal) — noble is not, and never was, a supported platform.

claim: NVIDIA Isaac Sim requires an RTX GPU with RT cores; a GeForce GTX 1660 SUPER (TU116) does NOT meet the minimum requirement.
correction:
The claim survives adversarial checking and is, if anything, understated — but two precision refinements are warranted:

(1) "Requires an RTX GPU" should be read as "requires an RT-core-equipped GPU," not strictly GeForce-RTX-branded. NVIDIA's own datacenter minimum in the IsaacSim README is an A40 (Ampere, RT cores, not "GeForce RTX"). The load-bearing requirement is RT cores, not the RTX brand string.

(2) "Does not meet the minimum requirement" is true on TWO independent axes, not just RT cores — and the VRAM axis is the harder gate. GTX 1660 SUPER has 6 GB; Isaac Sim 6.0's stated minimum is 16 GB (RTX 4080), and even the older 4.5.0 minimum was 8 GB (RTX 3070). The card fails the VRAM floor even ignoring RT cores entirely.

One nuance that does NOT rescue the GTX 1660 SUPER but should be stated accurately, because a naive version of this claim is refutable: TU116 is Turing (compute capability 7.5), and Turing IS listed as a supported architecture in the Omniverse RTX Renderer's "Feature Support per GPU Architecture" table. The architectures NVIDIA lists as unsupported there are Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta — Turing is not among them. GTX 16-series also gained DXR ray-tracing capability via driver 425.31 (April 2019), executed on CUDA cores instead of RT cores. So unlike a GTX 1080 (Pascal), which hard-fails with an explicit "GPU doesn't support RTX" error and exits, a GTX 1660 SUPER may not be rejected at the architecture gate. Do not claim "Isaac Sim will refuse to launch because TU116 is an unsupported architecture" — that specific reasoning is wrong. The correct reasoning is that NVIDIA explicitly states "GPUs without RT Cores are not supported," that "the ability to run Omniverse SDKs on non-RTX GPUs is provided without any support guarantees," and that 6 GB VRAM is far below the 16 GB minimum. Unsupported plus ray tracing emulated on shader cores plus 6 GB VRAM equals not viable in practice.

Also worth flagging for downstream decisions: NVIDIA staff stated in IsaacSim GitHub Discussion #423 that the minimum GPU model is "a supported/testing boundary as opposed to a hard technical limitation," and that it is "not an 'all or nothing' situation." So the RTX 4080 figure is not a hard runtime gate, and someone could argue a below-spec card "might work." That argument does not help here: it applies to below-spec cards that still have RT cores and adequate VRAM (e.g., an RTX 3090), not to a 6 GB card with zero RT cores. NVIDIA's own docs are internally inconsistent on adjacent points (GitHub issue #311 documents the minimum being stated as RTX 3070 in Omniverse docs, RTX 4080 in the Isaac Sim repo, and a working T4 deployment in the GCP docs; and A100/H100 are called "not supported" in Isaac Sim requirements while appearing as supported in the RTX renderer architecture table). None of these inconsistencies move the GTX 1660 SUPER above the line.

Practical bottom line for the target machine: Isaac Sim is not a viable option on this hardware, and the RT-core/VRAM gap is a hardware fact that no driver fix changes. Note this is independent of — and more fundamental than — the machine's current broken NVIDIA driver state (Secure Boot blocking nvidia.ko). Repairing the driver via MOK enrollment would restore CUDA and general GPU rendering, but would still leave Isaac Sim out of reach.
evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCES CHECKED

1. Isaac Sim official requirements, latest (6.0) — docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/latest/installation/requirements.html
   GPU table: Minimum = GeForce RTX 4080 / 16 GB VRAM; Good = GeForce RTX 5080 / 16 GB; Ideal = RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell / 48 GB.
   Verbatim: "GPUs without RT Cores (A100, H100) are not supported."
   Verbatim: "GPUs with less than 16GB VRAM may be insufficient to run a complex scene rendering more than 16MP per frame."

2. Isaac Sim 4.5.0 requirements (earlier release, for version-drift check) — docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/4.5.0/installation/requirements.html
   Minimum = GeForce RTX 3070 / 8 GB; Good = RTX 4080 / 16 GB; Ideal = RTX Ada 6000 / 48 GB.
   Same verbatim note: "GPUs without RT Cores (A100, H100) are not supported."
   Confirms the RT-core exclusion is long-standing, not a new 6.0 addition, and that the minimum has RISEN over time (3070/8GB -> 4080/16GB), so the claim is not "outdated" in the direction of becoming more permissive.

3. IsaacSim GitHub README — github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacSim
   Minimum for local workstation: RTX 4080. Datacenter minimum: A40. (Both RT-core-equipped.)

4. Omniverse RTX Renderer, "Feature Support per GPU Architecture" — docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/materials-and-rendering/latest/rtx-renderer_architecture_support.html
   Supported architectures listed: Blackwell RTX Pro, Blackwell B200/B300, Hopper H100/H200/H800, Ada Lovelace, Ampere (RTX), Ampere A100/A30/A800, Turing.
   Verbatim: "Older GPU architectures such as Tesla, Fermi, Kepler, Maxwell, Pascal and Volta are not supported by the Omniverse RTX Renderer."
   Verbatim: "The ability to run Omniverse SDKs on non-RTX GPUs is provided without any support guarantees."
   -> This is the strongest available counter-evidence to a naive reading of the claim (Turing is listed supported; TU116 is Turing). It establishes that the correct basis for excluding the 1660 SUPER is the RT-core/VRAM statement, not architecture-level rejection.

5. Omniverse technical requirements — docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/materials-and-rendering/latest/common/technical-requirements.html
   Minimum GPU for Kit applications: GeForce RTX 3070. Repeats the "non-RTX GPUs ... without any support guarantees" language.

6. NVIDIA Developer Forums, "GPU Requirement" (thread 305727) — NVIDIA staff (VickNV)
   Verbatim: "GPUs without RT Cores (e.g., A100, H100) are not supported."

7. IsaacSim GitHub Discussion #423, "Logic behind the minimum GPU spec" — NVIDIA staff
   Verbatim: "The minimum GPU requirement is defined by the lowest spec GPU tested for the given release. As you mentioned, it's a supported/testing boundary as opposed to a hard technical limitation."
   Verbatim: "It's not an 'all or nothing' situation."
   Steelmans the opposing view; does not overturn the RT-core/VRAM failure.

8. IsaacSim GitHub Issue #311, "Inconsistent documentation re. minimum GPU"
   Documents three conflicting NVIDIA statements of the minimum: RTX 4080 (repo/requirements), RTX 3070 (Omniverse technical requirements), and a working single-T4 install (GCP deployment docs). Establishes NVIDIA's docs are not fully self-consistent — but no source anywhere places the floor below an RT-core GPU.

9. NVIDIA Developer Forums, "Isaac Sim without RTX" (thread 158002)
   GTX 1080 user reports the app errors that the GPU does not support RTX and exits. NVIDIA staff (ltorabi) reply: "You can run it from the cloud." Note: GTX 1080 is Pascal, an explicitly unsupported architecture, so this is not directly transferable to TU116 — cited for completeness, not as proof for the 1660 SUPER.

10. Hardware fact, GTX 16-series / TU116 (Wikipedia GeForce 16 series; NVIDIA driver 425.31 coverage, April 2019)
    The GTX 16 series uses the same Turing architecture as RTX 20 but "omit[s] the Tensor (AI) and RT (ray tracing) cores exclusive to the 20 series." GTX 1660 = TU116, 1408 shaders, 192-bit bus. Driver 425.31 enabled DXR on GTX 1660 and above, with ray tracing executed on CUDA/shader cores — substantially slower and less efficient than dedicated RT cores.

SYNTHESIS
Both halves of the claim hold. NVIDIA states in the Isaac Sim requirements for every release checked (4.5.0 through 6.0) that GPUs without RT Cores are not supported, and every Minimum/Good/Ideal entry is an RT-core GPU. The GTX 1660 SUPER (TU116) has no RT cores and 6 GB VRAM, versus a stated minimum of RTX 4080 / 16 GB in current Isaac Sim 6.0. It fails the requirement on RT cores and independently on VRAM, and sits several generations below the minimum model. The only genuine imprecision in the claim is the implication that "RTX/RT cores" is the sole disqualifier and that TU116 would be rejected as an unsupported architecture — Turing is in fact listed as supported, so the accurate grounds are the explicit RT-core exclusion, the "no support guarantees" language for non-RTX GPUs, and the VRAM shortfall.

claim: There is no actively-maintained, official Livox MID-70 non-repetitive-scan sensor plugin for Gazebo Harmonic (gz-sim 8); the well-known livox_laser_simulation projects target Gazebo Classic.
correction:
Confirmed as stated. Two refinements for precision, neither of which overturns it:

(1) "No plugin at all for modern Gazebo" would be slightly too strong — unofficial gz-sim ports do exist, but none satisfies the claim's qualifiers. The closest is github.com/jongbob1918/livox_mid360_gz_sim_ros2 (1 star, last push 2026-07-16), whose own README states it is verified only on Ubuntu 22.04 / ROS 2 Humble / Gazebo **Fortress** and that "Gazebo Garden and Harmonic CMake discovery code is included but runtime verification is not yet complete." It is Mid-360 only, not MID-70, and not official. Also github.com/DHA-Tappuri/livox_ignition (1 star, 2025-04-03, Ignition Fortress).

(2) The Classic forks span two Classic generations, not one: the official Livox-SDK repo targets Gazebo 9.18 / ROS Melodic / Ubuntu 18.04, while the more recent community forks (ttwards/livox_gazebo_ros2_gpu_simulation, inkccc/mid360_simulation, ctu-mrs and fratopa Mid360 plugins) target Gazebo 11 / ROS 2 Humble. All are Gazebo Classic, which reached EOL in January 2025.

Additional load-bearing fact the claim does not state but which strengthens it: this is not merely a "nobody ported it" gap — stock gz-sim 8 is structurally incapable of expressing a non-repetitive pattern (see evidence), so a Harmonic plugin would require a custom gz::sim::System doing its own ray casting, not an SDF configuration.
evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCES CHECKED (all as of 2026-07-24):

1. OFFICIAL PLUGIN IS GAZEBO CLASSIC AND DORMANT — github.com/Livox-SDK/livox_laser_simulation
   - README "Requirements" verbatim: "ROS(=Melodic) / Gazebo (= 9.x, http://gazebosim.org/) / Ubuntu(=18.04)", plus "Note that the version of gazebo in main branch is gazebo 9.18. If you use gazebo 7, checkout to 'gazebo7' branch."
   - GitHub API: pushed_at = 2023-11-20, archived = false, 335 stars, 26 open issues. No commits in ~2.7 years.
   - Branch list is exactly ['gazebo7', 'main'] — no ignition/gz/harmonic branch exists.
   - MID-70 IS supported there (scan_mode/mid70.csv listed among HAP/mid360/avia/horizon/mid40/mid70/tele), but only under Classic 9.x.
   - Livox-SDK org front page shows no modern-Gazebo simulation repo; simulation is not among its pinned/active projects.

2. ALL WELL-KNOWN FORKS ARE CLASSIC
   - stm32f303ret6/livox_laser_simulation_RO2 (218 stars, pushed 2023-10-19), self-described "A ROS2 package to provide gazebo-classic plugin for Livox Series LiDAR".
   - LCAS/livox_laser_simulation_ros2 — same "gazebo-classic" description.
   - ttwards/livox_gazebo_ros2_gpu_simulation (9 stars, 2025-10-13) — README System Requirements: "Ubuntu 22.04 (Jammy), ROS2 Humble, Gazebo 11, SDFormat 9". Its support table lists Mid-70 (scan_mode/mid70.csv, urdf/mid70.xacro) explicitly marked "Untested"; only Mid-360 is "Tested".
   - inkccc/mid360_simulation (13 stars, 2026-01-13) — dependencies "ROS2 (Humble/Foxy), Gazebo 11, gazebo_ros_pkgs".
   - ctu-mrs/Mid360_simulation_plugin and fratopa/Mid360_simulation_plugin — ROS Noetic / Gazebo 11.

3. UPSTREAM GAZEBO HAS NO NATIVE NON-REPETITIVE LIDAR SUPPORT
   - gz-sim issue #1958 "Custom lidar sensor" (github.com/gazebosim/gz-sim/issues/1958) asks for exactly this: Livox "rosette"-type patterns, per-ray inclination angles from the CSV files, GPU-accelerated ~100k pts/s. Opened 2023-04-04. Verified state: still OPEN, with no linked branches or pull requests. Reporter notes it cannot be done as it was in Gazebo Classic's GpuRayPlugin.
   - DECISIVE SCHEMA EVIDENCE: SDF 1.11 lidar.sdf (sdformat14, the SDFormat shipped with Harmonic), fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com/gazebosim/sdformat/sdf14/sdf/1.11/lidar.sdf. The complete <scan> grammar is <horizontal>{samples, resolution, min_angle, max_angle} and optional <vertical>{samples, resolution, min_angle, max_angle}. There is NO element for arbitrary per-ray directions and no custom/CSV pattern element. A stock gz-sim 8 gpu_lidar can therefore only produce a uniform angular grid.

4. THE DOCUMENTED HARMONIC WORKAROUND IS AN APPROXIMATION, NOT THE REAL PATTERN
   - lxrobotics.com/blog/livox-mid-360-gazebo/ (written against Gazebo Harmonic 8.6.0) states the vendor plugin "can no longer be used, as only Gazebo Classic is supported," and recommends the built-in gpu_lidar configured as 720 horizontal samples / 40 vertical samples / 360 deg HFOV / 59 deg VFOV — i.e. a conventional uniformly-sampled spinning-lidar grid, explicitly not the non-repetitive scan pattern.

5. MID-70 IS DOUBLY LEGACY (context for why no official Harmonic plugin is likely)
   - MID-70 is a first-generation device served by Livox-SDK/livox_ros_driver (last push 2024-01-25) and livox_ros2_driver (2024-12-17). The current-generation Livox-SDK2 / livox_ros_driver2 stack explicitly supports only HAP and Mid-360. Livox's own active development has moved off the MID-70 line entirely, so all recent community simulation effort targets Mid-360.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT (Ubuntu 24.04 + Harmonic + ROS 2 Jazzy): reproducing MID-70 non-repetitive scanning on gz-sim 8 requires writing a custom gz::sim::System plugin that ray-casts the mid70.csv pattern itself (the CSV from the Classic repos is reusable). Otherwise the realistic options are a uniform gpu_lidar approximation of the MID-70's ~70.4 deg circular FOV, or staying on Gazebo Classic 11 (EOL since Jan 2025). Note the GTX 1660 SUPER/driver situation is orthogonal but relevant: gpu_lidar needs a working GPU render path, which is currently falling back to the Intel iGPU.

claim: AgileX publishes ROS 2 packages for the SCOUT MINI including a URDF/xacro description with meshes, but its Gazebo simulation packages target Gazebo Classic rather than gz-sim Harmonic.
correction: Both assertions hold, but the claim is imprecise in a way that matters operationally. Refined statement: "AgileX publishes ROS 2 packages for the SCOUT MINI, but the driver repo and the description are split. agilexrobotics/scout_ros2 (default branch 'humble'; also main/jazzy/humble_test) provides scout_base + scout_msgs with real mini support (scout_mini_base.launch.py, scout_mini_omni_base.launch.py) — but its scout_description package contains ONLY scout_v2 geometry and NO scout_mini URDF/xacro or mini mesh. The SCOUT MINI URDF/xacro with meshes lives in the SIMULATION repo agilexrobotics/ugv_gazebo_sim, branch 'humble', at scout/scout_description/. That simulation package targets Gazebo Classic 11 (not merely 'Gazebo Classic' generically), and the repo's DEFAULT master branch is older still — ROS 1 Melodic / Ubuntu 18.04. Critically for an Ubuntu 24.04 (noble) target: Gazebo Classic 11 has no noble binaries and is EOL, and ros-humble-gazebo-* does not exist on noble, so these packages are not installable as-published; per REP-2000 Jazzy pairs with Harmonic (Humble pairs with Classic 11 / Fortress). The mini xacro's <gazebo> blocks and skid-steer plugin require porting to gz-sim."
evidence:
PART 1 (ROS 2 packages + URDF/xacro with meshes) — TRUE but split across two repos:

- GitHub API on agilexrobotics/scout_ros2: default_branch=humble, pushed_at=2025-04-25T06:41:53Z, desc "ROS2 Support Package for Scout Robot". Branches: humble_test, humble, main, origin/jazzy.
- Top-level (humble/main/jazzy identical): scout_base, scout_description, scout_msgs.
- scout_ros2@humble scout_base/launch/ = scout_base.launch.py, scout_mini_base.launch.py, scout_mini_omni_base.launch.py -> mini DRIVER support confirmed.

claim: On Ubuntu with Secure Boot enabled, DKMS-built NVIDIA kernel modules are signed with a machine-owner key that must be enrolled with mokutil and confirmed at the blue MOK Manager screen during reboot — this cannot be completed non-interactively.
correction:
The mechanism is described correctly, but the conclusion is overstated in a way that matters operationally for this machine.

WHAT IS CORRECT:
1. DKMS-built NVIDIA modules on Ubuntu are auto-signed with a MOK. Canonical's security docs: "the installation of any new DKMS module (third-party driver) proceeds to sign the built module with the MOK." Verified on the target box: /lib/modules/6.8.0-136-generic/updates/dkms/nvidia.ko.zst has signer "ubuntu Secure Boot Module Signature key" (key pair at /var/lib/shim-signed/mok/MOK.priv + MOK.der), and `mokutil --list-enrolled` shows ONLY "Canonical Ltd. Master Certificate Authority" — i.e. the MOK is generated but not enrolled, which is exactly why nvidia.ko is refused.
2. Enrollment is confirmed at a blue MOK-management screen at the NEXT boot. Ubuntu wiki UEFI/SecureBoot/DKMS: "Reboot the system and press any key when you see the blue screen (MOK management)". Ubuntu security docs: "MokManager ... presents a set of text-mode panels allowing you to enroll the generated MOK at first boot. Select Enroll MOK, view the certificate fingerprint, and confirm enrollment."
3. That confirmation step itself genuinely requires a human at the physical console — this is deliberate shim design, not a bug. Ubuntu docs: "Most of these operations require user authentication, so the user must configure a password during the previous boot phase."

WHAT IS WRONG OR IMPRECISE:
A. "must be enrolled with mokutil" is imprecise. On Ubuntu the normal path is the shim-signed/dkms debconf prompt, or `sudo update-secureboot-policy --enroll-key`; `sudo mokutil --import <key>` is the manual equivalent. mokutil only QUEUES the request (MokNew); it does not enroll.
B. The load-bearing error: the sentence implies you cannot get the NVIDIA driver working under Secure Boot without a console visit. That is FALSE. Canonical ships pre-built, Canonical-signed NVIDIA kernel modules that require NO MOK at all, because they are signed by Canonical's key chaining to the Canonical Master CA that IS already enrolled on this machine. Ubuntu Server docs state flatly: "the DKMS drivers are not signed with Canonical's key and thus do not support secure boot", and ubuntu-drivers "will, by default, only install the pre-built, signed drivers which are known to work with Secure Boot."
   Verified against this machine's own apt indexes, for the exact running kernel 6.8.0-136-generic (noble-updates/restricted + noble-security/restricted):
     linux-modules-nvidia-580-generic              6.8.0-136.136+1
     linux-modules-nvidia-580-6.8.0-136-generic    6.8.0-136.136+1
     linux-objects-nvidia-580-6.8.0-136-generic    6.8.0-136.136+1
     linux-signatures-nvidia-6.8.0-136-generic     6.8.0-136.136+1
   `apt-get -s install linux-modules-nvidia-580-generic` resolves cleanly: 4 new, 0 removed. Its dependency `nvidia-kernel-common-580 (>= 580.173.02)` is already satisfied by the installed 580.173.02-0ubuntu0.24.04.1 userspace. So a fully non-interactive, SSH-only remedy exists: install those packages and reboot. Zero MOK, zero MokManager, zero physical presence.
   (The -generic-hwe-24.04 variant at 7.0.0-28.28~24.04.1+3 is the wrong one here — it tracks the HWE kernel, not the running 6.8 GA kernel.)
C. Critical caveat on that remedy: the Canonical-signed modules install to /lib/modules/6.8.0-136-generic/kernel/nvidia-580/, while depmod search order on this box is `search updates ubuntu built-in` (/etc/depmod.d/ubuntu.conf). `updates/` wins, so the unloadable MOK-signed DKMS module would still shadow the good one. nvidia-dkms-550 and nvidia-dkms-580 must be purged (this will also pull nvidia-driver-580, whose Depends includes `nvidia-dkms-580 (>= 580.173.02)`; keep nvidia-utils-580 / libnvidia-* explicitly).
D. Also note the claim's implicit escape hatches are NOT non-interactive either: `mokutil --disable-validation` requires the same blue MokManager screen, and disabling Secure Boot in firmware requires physical BIOS access. The Canonical-signed prebuilt module route is the ONLY headless option. Reason the MOK path cannot be automated on bare metal: MokList is a Boot-Services-only UEFI variable the running OS cannot write; automated pre-enrollment only exists for VM firmware varstores (e.g. OVMF via virt-fw-vars), which does not apply here.
E. Cosmetic: "blue" is Ubuntu's own documented wording, but the color is a firmware console attribute and renders differently on some systems. Also it is the NEXT boot, not "during reboot", and if not completed the request is discarded and must be re-issued.
evidence:
PRIMARY SOURCES:
1. Ubuntu security documentation, "UEFI Secure Boot" (documentation.ubuntu.com/security/security-features/platform-protections/secure-boot/, last updated Jan 22 2026, CC-BY-SA, Canonical Ltd.):
   - "In all cases, once the system runs with UEFI Secure Boot enabled and a recent version of shim, the installation of any new DKMS module (third-party driver) proceeds to sign the built module with the MOK. This happens without user interaction if a valid MOK key exists on the system and appears to be enrolled."
   - "If no MOK exists or the existing MOK isn't enrolled, a new key is automatically created just before signing, and you are prompted to enroll the key by providing a password required upon reboot."
   - "MokManager ... presents a set of text-mode panels allowing you to enroll the generated MOK at first boot. Select Enroll MOK, view the certificate fingerprint, and confirm enrollment."
   - "MokManager provides a console for users to enroll new public keys ... Most of these operations require user authentication, so the user must configure a password during the previous boot phase. This password is valid for a single run of shim and MokManager and is cleared as soon as the process completes or is canceled."
   - "the generated MOK key is kept on the filesystem as regular files owned by root with read-only permissions."
2. Ubuntu wiki, UEFI/SecureBoot/DKMS (last edited 2018-06-26 by cyphermox; fetched via curl, WebFetch got 503):
   - "Reboot the system and press any key when you see the blue screen (MOK management)"
   - "run sudo update-secureboot-policy --enroll-key to step through the enrollment wizard, or do the enrollment yourself by running sudo mokutil --import <your key>."
   - "In order to make DKMS work, Secure Boot signing keys for the system must be imported in the system firmware, otherwise Secure Boot needs to be disabled."
3. Ubuntu Server documentation, "NVIDIA drivers installation" (ubuntu.com/server/docs/how-to/graphics/install-nvidia-drivers/):
   - "the DKMS drivers are not signed with Canonical's key and thus do not support secure boot"
   - ubuntu-drivers is "recommended if your computer uses Secure Boot, since it will, by default, only install the pre-built, signed drivers which are known to work with Secure Boot."
4. NVIDIA GPU Operator docs, "Installing Precompiled and Canonical Signed Drivers on Ubuntu" (docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/gpu-operator/install-precompiled-signed-drivers.html): "This is required when nodes are enabled with Secure Boot."

DIRECT MEASUREMENTS ON THE TARGET MACHINE:
- `modinfo -F signer /lib/modules/6.8.0-136-generic/updates/dkms/nvidia.ko.zst` -> "ubuntu Secure Boot Module Signature key"; sig_key 0A:84:1E:99:C1:C6:4F:9A:0B:4D:93:56:EF:87:0F:D6:25:FC:1D:20
- /var/lib/shim-signed/mok/ contains MOK.der and MOK.priv
- `mokutil --list-enrolled` -> only "CN=Canonical Ltd. Master Certificate Authority" (no MOK enrolled) -> confirms the failure mode
- installed: dkms 3.0.11-1ubuntu13, mokutil 0.6.0-2build3, shim-signed 1.58+15.8-0ubuntu1, nvidia-dkms-550 550.163.01-0ubuntu0.24.04.2, nvidia-dkms-580 580.173.02-0ubuntu0.24.04.1, nvidia-driver-580 + nvidia-kernel-common-580 580.173.02-0ubuntu0.24.04.1
- /etc/dkms/framework.conf has no uncommented settings (signing comes from dkms defaults + /var/lib/shim-signed/mok)
- `apt-cache policy` confirms Canonical-signed exact-kernel packages available at 6.8.0-136.136+1 from noble-updates/restricted and noble-security/restricted: linux-modules-nvidia-580-generic, linux-modules-nvidia-580-6.8.0-136-generic, linux-objects-nvidia-580-6.8.0-136-generic, linux-signatures-nvidia-6.8.0-136-generic
- `apt-get -s install linux-modules-nvidia-580-generic` -> "0 upgraded, 4 newly installed, 0 to remove" (clean resolution)
- `dpkg-deb -c linux-objects-nvidia-580-6.8.0-136-generic_6.8.0-136.136+1_amd64.deb` -> installs to ./lib/modules/6.8.0-136-generic/kernel/nvidia-580/ (ships .o objects + BUILD script; the detached Canonical signature comes from linux-signatures-nvidia-6.8.0-136-generic)
- /etc/depmod.d/ubuntu.conf -> "search updates ubuntu built-in", proving updates/dkms/ shadows kernel/nvidia-580/ (basis for caveat C)

NOT FOUND / HEDGED: no primary quote located stating in so many words that MokList is Boot-Services-only and therefore unwritable from a running OS; that sub-point rests on shim design discussion (rhboot/shim MokManager.c, LKML "Enroll kernel keys thru MOK" v4/v5 threads) rather than a single authoritative sentence. It does not change the verdict, since Ubuntu's own docs independently establish that enrollment requires confirmation at the console.

claim: Gazebo Harmonic (gz-sim 8) provides segmentation and bounding-box camera sensors that can emit per-object ground truth usable for training vision models.
correction:
The claim is accurate as stated and I could not refute it. Five qualifications that matter for planning, none of which falsify it:

(1) NOT NEW IN HARMONIC. Both sensors shipped in Fortress (gz-sensors 6, 2021-2022) and Harmonic inherits them. The official Harmonic release-features page does not list them as Harmonic features; they appear under Fortress. "Provides" is still true.

(2) LABELS ARE NOT AUTOMATIC. The segmentation camera emits nothing until you manually tag each model/visual/include with the Label system plugin (`<plugin filename="gz-sim-label-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Label"><label>N</label></plugin>`). Untagged geometry is treated as background. For an orchard world with many tree/fruit models this is real authoring work, and label IDs are uint8 (0-255) since the labels map is RGB_INT8.

(3) "PER-OBJECT" IS ONLY TRUE IN THE RIGHT MODE. `<segmentation_type>semantic</segmentation_type>` gives per-CLASS masks, not per-object. Per-object requires `instance` / `panoptic`, where the labels map packs the label in the last channel and the instance count in the first two channels.

(4) 3D BOUNDING BOXES HAVE AN OPEN CORRECTNESS BUG IN HARMONIC. gz-sensors issue #428 ("BBox Camera seems to incorrectly rotate Coordinates"), opened 2024-05-06 against a Harmonic binary build, is still OPEN: 3D detections come out rotated ~180 degrees with negative z, i.e. objects reported behind the camera. Treat `<box_type>3d</box_type>` ground truth as untrustworthy until validated; `visible_2d` and `full_2d` are the safer paths.

(5) OGRE2 ONLY, WHICH COLLIDES WITH THIS MACHINE'S STATE. gz-rendering 8 implements these solely as Ogre2BoundingBoxCamera.cc / Ogre2SegmentationCamera.cc; there are no ogre1 equivalents (confirmed 404). So the ogre1 fallback is unavailable and a working OpenGL 3.3+ path is mandatory. With nvidia.ko blocked by Secure Boot lockdown and rendering falling back to the Intel AlderLake-S iGPU, these sensors should still function under Mesa but at throughput poor enough to matter for bulk dataset generation. Fixing the driver (enroll a MOK, or purge nvidia-driver-550 so DKMS/580 is coherent) is a prerequisite for this to be practical, not optional.

One additional planning note: ROS 2 bridging of 2D detections exists on ros_gz's jazzy/ros2 branches (vision_msgs/Detection2DArray <-> gz.msgs.AnnotatedAxisAligned2DBox_V) but the humble branch README lists only Detection3D/Detection3DArray. Pair Harmonic with Jazzy, not Humble, if you want 2D box bridging out of the box.
evidence:
SEGMENTATION CAMERA IN HARMONIC:
- Official tutorial https://gazebosim.org/api/sensors/8/segmentationcamera_igngazebo.html (gz-sensors 8 = Harmonic) documents `<sensor type="segmentation">`, semantic and panoptic/instance modes, publishing gz::msgs::Image on `<topic>/labels_map` and `<topic>/colored_map`, and the gz-sim-label-system plugin requirement.
- Source exists: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/gz-sensors8/src/SegmentationCameraSensor.cc — confirms topic suffixes "/colored_map" and "/labels_map", accepts segmentation_type of "semantic" | "instance" | "panoptic", publishes msgs::PixelFormatType::RGB_INT8, and saves to /colored_maps and /labels_maps folders.
- Encoding per https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gazebosim/gz-rendering/gz-rendering8/include/gz/rendering/SegmentationCamera.hh: "If the segmentation type is panoptic, the first two channels are the instance count, and the last channel is the label." Plus SetBackgroundLabel/SetBackgroundColor for unlabeled items.

BOUNDING BOX CAMERA IN HARMONIC:
- Class confirmed present in gz-sensors 8.2.2: https://gazebosim.org/api/sensors/8/classgz_1_1sensors_1_1BoundingBoxCameraSensor.html
- Source https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/gz-sensors8/src/BoundingBoxCameraSensor.cc (719 lines) shows: checks `_sdf.Type() != sdf::SensorType::BOUNDINGBOX_CAMERA`; box types BBT_VISIBLEBOX2D (default), BBT_FULLBOX2D, BBT_BOX3D; advertises msgs::AnnotatedOriented3DBox_V for 3D and msgs::AnnotatedAxisAligned2DBox_V otherwise (these are the per-object, label-carrying ground-truth messages); plus an `_image` companion topic and SaveImage()/SaveBoxes() writing /images and /boxes dataset folders when SaveFrames() is set.
- NOTE: gz-sensors 8 tutorial index (https://gazebosim.org/api/sensors/8/tutorials.html) lists only Introduction, Installation, Custom sensors, Thermal Camera, Segmentation Camera — there is NO bounding-box tutorial page for v8 (both .../sensors/8/boundingbox_camera.html and .../boundingbox_camera_igngazebo.html return 404; the tutorial exists only at .../sensors/9/...). This is a docs gap only; the code and example world are present in 8.

GZ-SIM 8 WIRES BOTH UP:
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gazebosim/gz-sim/gz-sim8/src/systems/sensors/Sensors.cc includes gz/sensors/BoundingBoxCameraSensor.hh and SegmentationCameraSensor.hh, and constructs them at lines ~1155-1163 on sdf::SensorType::BOUNDINGBOX_CAMERA and sdf::SensorType::SEGMENTATION_CAMERA.
- Shipped example worlds fetched (HTTP 200) from gz-sim8: examples/worlds/boundingbox_camera.sdf has three sensors `type="boundingbox_camera"` with `<box_type>` of full_2d, visible_2d, 3d; examples/worlds/segmentation_camera.sdf has `type="segmentation"` sensors with segmentation_type instance and semantic, plus multiple gz-sim-label-system plugin blocks with labels 30 and 40.

RENDER-ENGINE CONSTRAINT (raw URL HTTP status checks against gz-rendering8):
- 200 ogre2/src/Ogre2BoundingBoxCamera.cc
- 200 ogre2/src/Ogre2SegmentationCamera.cc
- 404 ogre/src/OgreBoundingBoxCamera.cc
- 404 ogre/src/OgreSegmentationCamera.cc

KNOWN DEFECT: https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sensors/issues/428 "BBox Camera seems to incorrectly rotate Coordinates", opened 2024-05-06 against Harmonic binary, state OPEN, 3D detections rotated 180 degrees / negative z.

ROS 2 BRIDGE: ros_gz_bridge README on branches jazzy and ros2 map vision_msgs/msg/Detection2D, Detection2DArray, Detection3D, Detection3DArray to gz.msgs.AnnotatedAxisAligned2DBox(_V) and AnnotatedOriented3DBox(_V). The humble branch README lists only the Detection3D/Detection3DArray pair.

RELEASE LINEAGE: https://gazebosim.org/docs/harmonic/release-features/ lists "Segmentation camera." and "Bounding box camera." under Fortress sensors, not as Harmonic-new features.
